sample_answers: The debugger allows us to view the values in the stack as the program runs. We can set a breakpoint and view the register values as the program moves along, something which cannot be easily done with printf. It also allowed us to see other register values that we may have not necessarily needed but became interested in later on, without needed to print out each and every register value.\n

While you can use printf, a debugger is faster and doesn’t require a recompile each time you want to observe a different value. It may also be more reliable since calling printf may cause values to change/be inaccurate. In addition, it may be hard to know exactly where register values are during runtime if you were to use printf, thus making the debugger an easier choice. Also, a debugger is specifically for debugging and viewing registers, not printf.\n

We used the debugger to view the memory that is being accessed. The debugger allows us to view the values of the different registers and where they are stored inside the memory. The debugger is used for this instead of a function like printf as one the debugger is a lower level program than printf has access to. Also using a function like printf would likely need to create new variables which would change values in the registers before it was able to print, thus it is much easier to use the debugger to view this instead.\n
Because the printf can’t show the registers’s value, and it can’t tell while the system is using psp or msp.\n

The debugger was used to allow us as students to step through our code and see as the register changes and allocates memory. When the program is started, the size of each stack had not been defined but as it is stepped through, the size of each stack adjusts accordingly which allows us to compare the value with what we had inputted. Printf would not show the exact value of the register. When we used the debugger, we were able to see that the size of MSP was off by a small value of bytes. Using printf, we would see the value that we assigned and the value that the microcontroller actually assigned.\n

The debugger is a useful tool that acts as a method to “view” the internal process of a code at various points of time. Specifically, it investigates data such as values of local and global variables, the order of function calls, and importantly, registers. The debugger uses a concept known as breakpoints, which is placed by the user before pressing the debug button. Its function is to allow the program to run the debugging process and stop at each indicated breakpoint, where the variable and register values can be viewed AT the moment where the code hit the breakpoint. This allows users to identify exactly where errors were made in the program. In this lab, it was important that the debugger tool displayed the values of all the registers at the desired breakpoint. These registers include the registers r0 to r12, sp, pc, and xpsr. In the lab we used the debugger to view the register that stores the address of variables MSP and PSP values to see if they were spaced properly in the stack that was created. Simply using the printf function to check values isn’t as efficient, printf only displays as many outputs at one instance, which doesn’t grant as much flexibility as the debugger with breakpoints. Furthermore, using printf functions can potentially alter the behaviour of the general code.\n

The reason we used the debugger in this lab is because it allows us to pause the code at specific points to check register values and variable changes; in the case of this code, it’s at the while loop. The use of the debugger allows us to see the change throughout the code, before and after the stopping points. If we just used printf, then we would not be able to determine at what point in the code variable values or register values change. With the debugger, we can look at the stack pointer and memory before and after pause to see how the code is setting up and using memory while it runs.\n

We needed to use the debugger in this lab to view the values of the registers and of the stack itself in a neat and organized way. Using printf to instrument our code is more time consuming and can affect the registers themselves.\n

The debugger was used instead of printf statements because printf cannot reliably print the values of registers such as SP, MSP, PSP during runtime operation. As such, breaks were needed in the code using the debugging tool to see the values of the registers as the code was stepped through.\n

The debugger was used to access processor-specific information, such as register values and stack pointers, which are not visible through printf. Registers like MSP and PSP require direct inspection for validation and cannot be reliably output via software printing. The debugger provides a real-time view of the internal processor state, enabling accurate analysis of memory usage, function behavior, and hardware-level execution. In contrast, printf is limited to displaying user-defined variables and lacks the resolution needed for detailed system-level observation.\n

We must use the debugger in this lab because we must pause the execution of the program. The program constantly pushes and pops data to and from the stack. As a result, the memory location of the stack is continuously changing. The printf function will most likely not work to validate our code as we need to compare the memory locations of multiple registers whose locations may change during the execution of printf. By using the debugger to freeze the execution, we can ensure that the memory locations of the registers shown by the debugger are all from the exact same point in the execution, so we can accurately compare them.\n

Debugger stops the code midway for us to look at the registers and variables. This shows the value of MSP_INITIAL_VAL changing throughout the code, prior to run and after. When just running printf, we would not be able to carefully see which lines of code changes the values of certain variables or register values. With the debugger, we can inspect the stack pointer values and verify changes before reaching the while(1) loop. This gives us precise visibility into how the stack is set up and how memory is being allocated during execution\n

Using the debugger means that the register values of psp, msp, and sp—which can’t be printed to terminal or console—can be simultaneously tracked for each line of code, which helps resolve logic or runtime errors.\n

The debugger allows the value actual value of the stack to be observed, rather than just the end value. The registers window shows this in more depth. In this window, registers can be seen representing specific memory, and using the debugger allows the user to see what is being stored in that memory location at a specified break point. This is beneficial to understand what exactly is happening behind the scenes to achieve the end goal. In this lab we are looking to see the in between steps rather than the end value. Printf would only just provide the end value. This can be compared to using the registers, where the inbetween steps of the memory is not seen from printf. For example, if the variable value got overwritten somewhere in the code, and by using printf this only prints the overwritten value, but by using debugger and registers, it allows the user to find exactly where their mistake occurred.\n
We use the debugger to observe register activity, which cannot be reliably observed with printf.\n

We used the debugger to observe the Cortex-M4’s live memory while the program was running. In this lab, it allowed us to examine the actual contents of the stack at each step of code execution. This level of visibility is crucial because functions like printf are complex and can significantly alter the stack by the time they execute. As a result, relying on printf to inspect the stack could lead to misleading or overwritten data. By setting breakpoints, we were able to pause execution at precise moments and inspect the immediate memory state.\n

The debugger allows us to pause the program using the breakpoints. This allows us to look at memory and registers live as the values are changed. Printf only shows the end result without any information about when variables are changed or updated.\n

We used the debugger in this lab because it allows us to observe program variables and hardware registers in real time. In embedded systems, variables are values stored in RAM and managed by the program, while hardware registers are special memory-mapped locations used to control and monitor the behavior of hardware components, like timers, GPIO, or communication peripherals. A tool like printf can only display values that the software can access and is often limited to program variables. It usually cannot access or display hardware registers directly, especially if they require specific timing or access patterns. Additionally, printf only shows values after the fact and introduces delays that can interfere with timing-sensitive operations. In contrast, a debugger lets us pause the program at any point using breakpoints and inspect the current state of both variables and hardware registers. This provides much deeper insight into how the system is behaving, especially when we’re trying to understand low-level interactions between software and hardware.\n

Clarifying that the statement must refer specifically to "register values" removes ambiguity where a student mentions printf’s impact on the stack but does not tie it to registers, leading to consistent grading.

By tightening the criterion to require an explanation that directly connects printf’s limitations to register inspection, graders will uniformly recognise valid explanations and reject vague or unrelated statements, reducing inconsistency.

The debugger allows us to pause the program using the breakpoints. This allows us to look at memory and registers live as the values are changed. Printf only shows the end result without any information about when variables are changed or updated.\n

We used the debugger in this lab because it allows us to observe program variables and hardware registers in real time. In embedded systems, variables are values stored in RAM and managed by the program, while hardware registers are special memory-mapped locations used to control and monitor the behavior of hardware components, like timers, GPIO, or communication peripherals. A tool like printf can only display values that the software can access and is often limited to program variables. It usually cannot access or display hardware registers directly, especially if they require specific timing or access patterns. Additionally, printf only shows values after the fact and introduces delays that can interfere with timing-sensitive operations. In contrast, a debugger lets us pause the program at any point using breakpoints and inspect the current state of both variables and hardware registers. This provides much deeper insight into how the system is behaving, especially when we’re trying to understand low-level interactions between software and hardware.\n
